title: Changing Identities and Evolving Conceptions of Inquiry through Teacher-Driven Professional Development
extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-driven professional development program shaped secondary science teachers’ understanding of scientific inquiry and their participation in a professional community. The central problem is that teachers often hold ambiguous or incomplete conceptions of inquiry, and the authors ask whether sustained, collaborative, minimally facilitated professional development can help teachers develop a more coherent, expert-like shared understanding.

The intervention studied is Streamline to Mastery, a five-year professional development program in which teachers partner with university researchers to co-design professional learning. Teachers and researchers met every other week to share inquiry-oriented lessons, discuss classroom experiences, reflect on lessons, and plan conference presentations and other activities. The study analyzed lesson reflections, inquiry survey responses, videotaped meetings, email threads, and interviews, using both qualitative coding and frequency counts aligned with the NRC five essential features of inquiry.

The participants were four secondary physical science teachers from two urban high schools in the Rocky Mountain West of the United States. They taught in high-needs contexts, and most were teaching outside their primary science discipline. Over time, the teachers’ talk about inquiry became more aligned with the five essential features, while also preserving themes such as real-world relevance, ownership, and social construction of knowledge. The paper concludes that the program supported growth in teacher agency and leadership as teachers increasingly initiated emails, set agendas, and challenged one another’s ideas, and that shared, experience-grounded discourse was central to this development.
